analysis.one_liner: Makes gasoline price gouging illegal during federally declared energy emergencies.
analysis.headline: Backed by a Senate sponsor and 31 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal, during a presidentially declared energy emergency, to sell gasoline, crude oil, or petroleum products at prices that are unconscionably excessive or that take unfair advantage of a shortage. It gives the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general power to enforce that ban, with civil penalties up to $3 million and criminal penalties including up to five years in prison. It would also require more price transparency in wholesale fuel markets and direct periodic investigations of how much major oil companies and automakers have invested in alternative fuels. The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary drivers and households buying gasoline, heating fuel, and other petroleum products. During supply disruptions like hurricanes, when fuel is scarce and prices spike, consumers would gain a federal backstop against grossly inflated prices, enforced by the FTC and their own state attorneys general. Wholesale buyers and honest retailers would also benefit from better price transparency and from rules against false price reporting and market manipulation.

how_it_helps.text: During a declared energy emergency, selling gasoline, crude oil, or petroleum products at an unconscionably excessive price, or taking unfair advantage of a shortage to raise prices unreasonably, would be unlawful.

The bill considers a price unconscionable when it shows a gross disparity from pre-emergency prices or grossly exceeds what similar buyers in the area paid, while accounting for legitimate cost increases the seller could not control.

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban, with priority given to large companies selling more than $500 million a year in fuel, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents.

Violations of the price-gouging ban carry civil penalties up to $3 million and criminal penalties of up to a $1 million fine, five years' imprisonment, or both, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately.
It would also be unlawful to report false or misleading wholesale price data to the FTC or to use manipulative or deceptive devices in wholesale fuel purchases and sales.

The FTC would be directed to make wholesale crude oil and fuel prices more transparent to the public, states, and market participants, and to coordinate information-sharing with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The Comptroller General would investigate every four years how much major oil companies and automobile manufacturers have invested in alternative fuels production and infrastructure, and the National Academy of Sciences would review oil companies' spending to protect supply from disasters, including the forecasted more intense hurricane activity in the Gulf of Mexico.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies that sell fuel at sharply elevated prices during declared emergencies would face civil penalties of up to $3 million per violation, criminal exposure, and FTC enforcement scrutiny. Fuel sellers generally would bear new compliance risk and, under the transparency provisions, new reporting obligations. Automobile manufacturers and major oil companies would also face periodic federal investigations into their alternative-fuels investments. If anti-gouging rules discouraged suppliers from moving fuel into shortage areas, consumers in those areas could face tighter supply, a cost the bill tries to offset by allowing market-clearing prices as a mitigating factor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large oil companies and fuel sellers

drawbacks.text: Anti-gouging rules set by law rather than by the market can discourage suppliers from rerouting scarce fuel to the hardest-hit regions, since high prices are the signal that draws fuel where it is most needed; the bill tries to manage this by treating prices that reasonably equate supply and demand, or that reflect genuine cost increases outside the seller's control, as mitigating factors.

The whole scheme turns on a presidential declaration that an energy emergency exists, which a hostile administration could simply decline to make, leaving the protections dormant; the President may also renew a 45-day declaration repeatedly.

The penalties are large and the standard of 'unconscionably excessive' is judged after the fact against pre-emergency prices, which creates litigation risk for fuel sellers even when a price spike reflects real supply costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and broad: when storms or other disruptions knock out fuel supply, ordinary households are the ones who pay whatever the pump asks, and this bill would give federal and state enforcers a tool against grossly inflated prices while leaving state law untouched. The main honest cost is the classic one — legally penalizing high emergency prices risks blunting the price signal that pulls fuel into shortage areas — though the bill's own mitigating factors try to carve out genuine cost-based pricing. On balance the bill was a serious consumer-protection measure with manageable, largely design-level drawbacks, and it died without ever being tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 109th Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on September 20, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill attracted 31 cosponsors — 30 Democrats and the Senate's one Independent — within days of introduction.
No further action appears in the record: no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no House action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies came out ahead: they never faced the emergency price-gouging penalties, wholesale price transparency requirements, or periodic investigations of their alternative-fuel investments that the bill would have imposed. Consumers were left without a federal price-gouging backstop during the supply disruptions and high fuel prices of that period.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or the chamber's lone Independent — 30 Democrats, 1 Independent, no Republicans — and the Republican-run Commerce Committee and Republican Senate leadership never gave it a vote.

industries.note: The bill would make it unlawful to sell fuel at unconscionably excessive prices during declared energy emergencies, with civil penalties up to $3 million (counted per day for continuing violations) and criminal exposure, and would open their pricing to FTC transparency requirements and periodic federal investigations of their alternative-fuel and disaster-preparedness spending. Selling fuel at whatever price a shortage permits is where emergency-period profits come from, so the industry's interest ran directly against the consumers the bill was written for.

industries.industry: Wholesale fuel traders and price-reporting market participants
industries.note: The bill bans knowingly false wholesale price reporting to the FTC and manipulative or deceptive devices in wholesale fuel trading, and requires public dissemination of wholesale price and availability information. Traders and refiners profiting from opaque wholesale markets would lose that opacity.

The bill would require the Comptroller General to periodically investigate and report to Congress how much automakers have invested in alternative fuels production, infrastructure, and technology. The direct legal burden is small — a study, not a mandate — but it creates recurring public scrutiny of how much they have diversified consumer fuel options.
